description: Before 1846, an operation was often carried out consciously and in extreme pain. Anesthesia transforms surgery into care, not torture.

hero.hook: One day in 1846, in Boston, surgery ceased to be a race against pain.

blocks.text: Imagine an amputation without falling asleep. Before the mid-19th century, this was the norm. We strap the patient in, we move quickly, we pray.
**anesthesia** changes everything: it allows you to operate without awareness of pain. Modern surgery can finally take its time.

blocks.caption: Without anesthesia, the surgeon had to be extremely fast.

blocks.text: Surgeons were judged on their speed. Alcohol, opium, or brute force were used to immobilize people. Many patients died from shock, infection, or hemorrhage.

blocks.caption: In Boston, a public demonstration convinced the medical world.

blocks.text: **October 16, 1846**, in Boston, the dentist **William Morton** makes a patient inhale **ether**. Surgeon **John Warren** operates on a neck tumor. The patient is not screaming. The room is stunned.
Warren reportedly said, “Gentlemen, this is not a humbug.” The phrase has remained famous.

Other products followed, such as **chloroform**, popularized in particular in Great Britain. Rivalries arise over who “invented” what. The patent doesn't matter: the idea is spreading all over the world.
There remains one problem: to put to sleep without killing. You have to dose it, monitor your breathing and your heart. A new specialty is born.
Today, the anesthesiologist uses precise gases and drugs, machines that measure everything. You can put the whole body to sleep or just an area (local or locoregional anesthesia).
Since the demonstration of ether in **1846**, anesthesia has transformed surgery: less pain, more time, more precision... and safety has become a science in its own right.

subtitle: Medicine
title: The discovery of anesthesia
